ch-01: This guide explains a large body of work on computers, languages and intelligence. You can read it, run the programs on your own computer, or ask an AI to help you, and every example in it was really run.
ch-02: What matters is whether the work holds up, whether the code runs and the reasoning is sound, not who made it. The aim is that people build technology in their own languages.
ch-hist: This work began long before today's AI. It grew along five connected lines: languages and computers, learning machines, robots and medicine, organised knowledge, and the future of people and their homes.
ch-05: A list of what was made and when, from 1993 onwards, with where each item can be checked.
ch-03: One shared core, Humanesque, is seen through three cultures: Indian, Persian and Western. Around it sit the parts that turn an idea, in any language, into something real.
ch-graph: A map of how the parts connect, like a city map with roads between places. Any route you follow is one journey; the map is the whole picture.
ch-onto: A dictionary of the special words used here, each with the nearest everyday idea and what makes it different.
ch-acts: Three stages of one long story: machines that think with us; machines that help us build with living, synthetic and natural materials; and people and their worlds carrying on into the future.
ch-families: Three groups explained one at a time: the AyeAI Triad of thinking, body and communication; GramSheel and Project VIKRAM for villages; and Humanesque with the names it takes in each culture.
ch-04: A catalogue of every public project folder, what each one does, and its permanent reference number where it has one.
ch-06: Which computer set-up to use: Linux works best, Windows works through WSL, and a Mac works for most things.
ch-07: How to install the basic tools and run your first real program from this work.
ch-run: Step-by-step commands to start each part on your own computer, with what you should see when it works and what to do when it does not.
ch-08: How a container packs a whole laboratory into one box that runs the same on every computer, and what comes next.
ch-09: How a computer stores numbers using only ones and zeros, including negative numbers and fractions.
ch-10: How letters from any script become numbers inside a computer, and why a name must survive every tool a program passes through.
ch-11: How Romenagri turns Indian scripts into plain English letters and back again without losing anything, and why Urdu written without its vowel marks is harder.
ch-12: Pāṇini's grammar of Sanskrit, written well over two thousand years ago, works like a computer program, and this chapter runs part of it.
ch-13: How a program written in Hindi or Urdu becomes instructions a machine can run, with every name kept intact all the way to the debugger.
ch-14: What happens inside chips: switches, circuits, three-valued logic, and the very cold machines that hold qubits.
ch-15: How quantum computers work, and how a network of swinging oscillators can solve the same kind of puzzle.
ch-16: How AI grew from rule books to today's language models, and how to use any AI, safely, to help with this work.
ch-17: How to share, copy and improve this work in the open, and how each piece is stamped with its date and a permanent reference.
ch-18: India's national engineering examination: what it covers, how to apply, and why it is worth sitting at any age.
ch-19: Short technical answers to questions people often ask, such as whether AI needs English, and who controls it.
ch-20: What this edition contains, what changed in it, and what comes next.
app-a: A table matching the special terms used here with the closest common terms.
app-read: How to read the architecture without squashing it into a straight line: what an arrow can mean, and the loops that run at different scales.
app-hum: A guide for researchers in the humanities and social sciences: the questions each field can ask of this work, and where to find and test the answers.
app-stem: A guide for researchers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics: what can be read, run and tested now, and what is still open.
app-prac: A guide for teachers, policy makers, community workers, artists and engineers: where to start and how to take part.
app-refs: The books and papers this guide draws on.
ch-roadmap: The plan to finish the releases and open the work to everyone: what happens when, which lane each kind of person can join, and every field of work, from farming to medicine to software.
app-math: The same ideas written as mathematics, for readers who want the formal version.
ch-start: Four steps to find your part of the guide: who you are, your board or field, what you want to do, and your path with a PDF made for you.
ch-syllabus: Links from your school or exam syllabus to the chapters that teach the same ideas, worked out on your own device, and a draft syllabus of our own.
ch-projections: The names each culture gives the shared parts, with new names proposed for review, and the steps for raising a part into the common core.
ch-estimate: A measured estimate of how much work the estate holds and what it would cost to rebuild, with and without AI.
app-review: A list of every part of this guide, showing which parts the author has checked by hand.
